name: Battle of Kadesh
info: Ramesses II of Egypt and Muwatalli II of the Hittite Empire fought on the Orontes near Kadesh after a Hittite attack nearly broke the Egyptian army; both sides claimed victory and the Hittites kept Kadesh.

facts.date: Year 5, third month of Shemu, day 9 of Ramesses II, generally dated to May 1274 BCE by the low chronology; the high chronology puts it about 20 years earlier
facts.place: On the Orontes River upstream of Lake Homs, near the stronghold of Kadesh, on what is now the Lebanon-Syria border
facts.sides: The Egyptian Empire under Ramesses II, in four divisions (Amun, Re, Set and Ptah) with Sherden troops and the Ne'arin; the Hittite Empire under Muwatalli II with allies, among them Rimisharrinaa, king of Aleppo. Chariots on both sides together are put at 5,000 to 6,000
facts.outcome: The Egyptians drove the Hittites back across the Orontes, but the Hittites kept Kadesh. Modern historians describe a stalemate, and each side claimed the victory.

t: In the Egyptian account Ramesses II was misled by two nomads sent by the Hittites, and his army was attacked while strung out on the march.
Almost everything known about the battle comes from Egyptian inscriptions and reliefs, whose bombastic tone is recognised; the Hittite side survives only in scattered references.
Neither empire could defeat the other in Syria, and about 15 years later they made a peace treaty that survives in Hittite and Egyptian versions.
dyk: A large replica of the Egyptian-Hittite peace treaty of about 1258 BCE hangs at the headquarters of the United Nations, as the earliest international peace treaty known to historians.
ev: The Hyksos' 15th Dynasty is expelled and the rulers of the New Kingdom begin reclaiming Egypt's borders
Ramesses II leaves Pi-Ramesses with four divisions and marches along the coast through Gaza
Two Shasu nomads give Ramesses a false report that the Hittites are far off at Aleppo
Hittite chariots cross the Orontes, scatter the Re division and attack the Egyptian camp
An Egyptian counterattack, the arrival of the Ne'arin and the Ptah division drive the Hittites back to the river
Ramesses II and Hattusili III make a peace treaty in the 21st year of Ramesses' reign

sections.background:
After the expulsion of the Hyksos' 15th Dynasty around 1550 BCE, the rulers of the New Kingdom of Egypt grew more aggressive in reclaiming control of their borders. Thutmose I, Thutmose III and Amenhotep II fought from Megiddo north to the Orontes, including conflict with Kadesh. The Amarna letters tell of declining Egyptian influence, and under Thutmose IV and Amenhotep III Egypt lost territory to the Mitanni in northern Syria. Horemheb, who died in 1292 BCE, campaigned there again and turned Egyptian interest back to the area.

The Nineteenth Dynasty continued this. Seti I, like his father before him, set out to restore the empire of the Eighteenth Dynasty pharaohs. Inscriptions on the Karnak walls record his campaigns in Canaan and Syria; he made an informal peace with the Hittites, and a second campaign led to his capture of Kadesh and the kingdom of Amurru. His son Ramesses II campaigned with him. At some point both regions may have lapsed back under Hittite control. What happened to Amurru is disputed: the Hittitologist Trevor R. Bryce suggests that it more likely remained a Hittite vassal state.

In the fourth year of his reign Ramesses II marched into Syria, either to recapture Amurru or as a probe of his vassals' loyalty and of the terrain for battles. A large weapons order of the year before is recorded. He launched the expedition of his fifth year from his capital Pi-Ramesses (modern Qantir) in May 1274 BCE, passing the fortress of Tjaru and following the coast to Gaza. The Hittite king Muwatalli II gave the recovery of Amurru as his reason for marching south.
sections.forces:
Ramesses led an army of four divisions: Amun, Re, Set and the apparently newly formed Ptah division. A poorly documented troop called the Ne'arin, possibly Canaanite mercenaries or Egyptians, had been left in Amurru to secure the port of Sumur, and it was to play a critical part in the battle. Sherden troops also fought for Egypt, and this is the first record of them as Egyptian mercenaries; they later appear among the Sea Peoples who raided the eastern Mediterranean at the end of the Bronze Age.

The battle is believed to be the largest ever fought involving chariots, together 5,000 to 6,000. Mark Healy, in Armies of the Pharaohs, says the Egyptian chariot force cannot be stated precisely but could not have numbered fewer than 2,000 vehicles across the Amun, Re, Ptah and Set corps, on the assumption of about 500 in each, and that the Ne'arin's chariots may have to be added if they were not native Egyptian troops.

The Hittite king Muwatalli II had mustered several allies, among them Rimisharrinaa, king of Aleppo. Ramesses recorded a list of 19 allies whom Muwatalli brought to Kadesh, which interests Hittitologists because it shows how far Hittite influence reached. The Hittite king also hired local Shasu tribes. Muwatalli placed his troops behind "Old Kadesh", out of sight of the approaching Egyptians.
sections.course:
Ramesses' inscriptions say his advance guard, about 11 kilometres from Kadesh, met two Shasu nomads who said that the Hittite king was in the land of Aleppo, 200 kilometres away and too afraid of Pharaoh to come south. Egyptian texts call this a false report ordered by the Hittites. A scout then brought in two Hittite prisoners, who said that the whole Hittite army stood ready behind the old city of Kadesh. By then Ramesses was alone with his bodyguard and the Amun division, and the vizier was sent to hurry up the Ptah and Set divisions.

While he was meeting his princes, Hittite chariots crossed the river and struck the middle of the Re division as it marched towards him. Caught in the open, it scattered, some men fleeing north to the Amun camp with Hittite chariots behind them. The chariots then rounded north and attacked the camp, causing panic, but obstacles in the large camp slowed them. In the Egyptian account Ramesses was deserted and surrounded, called on Amun, and led several charges with his guard and survivors of the Re division.

The Hittites, believing the Egyptians routed, stopped to plunder the camp and were driven back towards the Orontes, where Egyptian chariots overtook them. Muwatalli, who still held reserves and the town walls, sent another thousand chariots forward. The Ne'arin then arrived suddenly from Amurru, and the Ptah division came up from the south, threatening the Hittite rear. After six unsuccessful Hittite charges the survivors, pinned against the river, left their chariots and tried to swim it, and many drowned, as Egyptian accounts tell it.
sections.aftermath:
The Hittites were routed but kept Kadesh. Ramesses could not support a long siege of the walled city, so he gathered his troops and went south towards Damascus and back to Egypt. He proclaimed that he had routed his enemies and had not tried to take Kadesh. The Egyptian account says the two armies faced each other again the next day, with a stalemate as the result. Hittite records from Hattusa give a different ending, in which Ramesses was forced to leave Kadesh in defeat. Hittite records indicate that at least two of Muwatalli's brothers were killed; a third brother, the future Hattusili III, probably fought there.

Muwatalli went on to campaign as far south as the Egyptian province of Upi, which he captured and placed under his brother Hattusili. Egypt's sphere of influence in Asia was restricted to Canaan, which was for a time threatened by revolts among Egypt's Levantine vassals. In his eighth and ninth years Ramesses took the Hittite-ruled cities of Dapur and Tunip, but the strip of land between Amurru and Kadesh could not be held and returned to Hittite control within a year, and he had to march against Dapur again in his tenth year. Neither Egypt nor Hatti could decisively defeat the other in the region.

A treaty with the new Hittite king Hattusili III was signed some 15 years after Kadesh, in the 21st year of Ramesses II (1258 BCE), and ended the borderland conflicts.
sections.sources:
There is more evidence in texts and wall reliefs for this battle than for any other in the Ancient Near East, but almost all of it is Egyptian. The main account is Ramesses' own, whose bombastic nature is recognised. It exists in two forms, the Poem and the Bulletin. The Poem has been questioned as true verse rather than a prose account like those of other pharaohs, and the Bulletin is a caption to the reliefs. The Bulletin is repeated seven times and the Poem eight, in temples at Abydos, Luxor, Karnak, Abu Simbel and the Ramesseum, and many small captions identify details of the scenes.

Further Egyptian evidence is in Papyrus Raifet and Papyrus Sallier III, and in a letter from Ramesses to Hattusili III answering Hattusili's complaint about the pharaoh's claims of victory. Hittite references, including that letter, have been found at Hattusa, but no annals describing the battle as part of a campaign have been found; it is mentioned in connection with other events, above all by Hattusili III, for whom it was a milestone in his career.

James Henry Breasted made the first scholarly reconstruction in 1903, from Egyptian sources. Historians disagree about who won. Trevor Bryce says both sides claimed victory: Ramesses had the upper hand at the end but failed to retake Amurru and Kadesh, the point of the dispute, so that he describes an Egyptian tactical victory on the field and a Hittite strategic one, since the Hittites kept the disputed territory. The date also depends on the chronology used, the high chronology placing it about 20 years earlier.
sections.legacy:
Kadesh is the earliest pitched battle in recorded history for which details of tactics and formations are known. Ramesses treated it as a personal triumph, the king who rallied his scattered troops after moving into an ambush, and he had the account carved on temple walls across Egypt. The Hittite court remembered it differently, and the letter from Hattusili III shows that the pharaoh's claims were contested between the two kings themselves.

Modern historians conclude that the battle ended in a draw in practical terms. It is held to be a turning point for the Egyptians, who had developed new technologies and rearmed against years of Hittite incursions. Egyptian influence over Amurru and Kadesh seems to have been lost for good, and Egypt's gains in Syria in the following years did not last.

Its best-known result is the treaty. It was inscribed on a silver tablet, of which a clay copy was found in the Hittite capital Hattusa, now in Turkey, and is on display at the Istanbul Archaeology Museum; an Egyptian version survives on papyrus. A large replica hangs at the headquarters of the United Nations. Peace brought intermarriage between the two courts, and Hattusili III and Ramesses II developed close relations.

summary: Near Kadesh on the Orontes in 1274 BCE, Ramesses II of Egypt and the Hittite king Muwatalli II fought a chariot battle that nearly broke the Egyptian army. Both kings claimed victory, the Hittites kept Kadesh, and about 15 years later the two empires made a treaty.
references: Mark Healy, Qadesh 1300 B.C, Clash of the Warrior Kings (Osprey Publishing, 1993)
Miriam Lichtheim, Ancient Egyptian Literature (University of California Press, 1976)
Ian Shaw, The Oxford History of Ancient Egypt (Oxford University Press, 2003)
notes: The article gives no total army sizes for either side; only the combined chariot figure of 5,000 to 6,000 and Healy's minimum of 2,000 Egyptian chariots. I added no figures from memory.
The article's date is Year 5, III Shemu day 9; the quoted Poem says 2nd month of the third season and the Bulletin 3rd month. I used the article's III Shemu day 9 and did not discuss the discrepancy.
The article names two killed Hittite brothers only in garbled transliteration, so I left the names out.
The next day's stalemate is told only in the Egyptian-side narrative ('the following day'); the article does not say who reports it, so my text says 'the Egyptian account'. Please check.
I wrote 'some 15 years' after, as the article does; the 1258 BCE treaty date in the last event is the article's.
Left out: the article's 'two heroes' remark about Hattusili and Ramesses (praise word), the long Poem quotation, and the Rimisharrinaa/19 allies' names.
